explanation.text: Jefferson sent Livingston to France in 1803 to negotiate New Orleans; Monroe joined him later that year. Multiple sources confirm both envoys were active in France in 1803 working on the New Orleans purchase.

Jefferson appointed Monroe as envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary to France in January 1803, and Livingston was the resident minister authorized to purchase territory including New Orleans. Monroe joined Livingston in Paris on April 12 after Livingston's negotiations were well under way

Livingston was dispatched immediately upon learning Spain had retroceded New Orleans and Louisiana to France, and Monroe's appointment in January 1803 set the diplomatic framework for the New Orleans acquisition

The coded midnight letter that foreshadowed the largest land transfer in US history

April 12, 1803
Livingston was one of two diplomats sent to Paris by President Thomas Jefferson to negotiate a purchase of New Orleans and its environs from France.
Jefferson had dispatched Livingston immediately upon learning that Spain had retroceded New Orleans and Louisiana to their original colonizer, France.

excerpts.text: Resolved to settle the matter by peaceful measures, President Jefferson in January 1803 appointed [Monroe](https://www.britannica.com/place/Monroe-county-New-York) envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary to France to aid [Robert R. Livingston](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Robert-R-Livingston), the resident minister, in purchasing the territory at the mouth of the Mississippi—including the island of New Orleans—authorizing him at the same time to cooperate with [Charles Pinckney](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-Pinckney), the minister at Madrid, in securing from Spain the cession of East and West Florida.

assessment.rationale: Span 91 states Monroe joined Livingston in Paris on April 12 after Livingston's negotiations were well under way. This confirms the event occurred in 1803 and in France, but places the meeting in April rather than the general timeframe of 1803.

excerpts.text: Monroe joined Livingston in Paris on April 12, after the latter’s negotiations were well under way, and the two ministers, on finding [Napoleon](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Napoleon-I) willing to dispose of the entire province of Louisiana, decided to [exceed](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/exceed) their instructions and effect its purchase.
